16.6.1 The geometry of the RKHS
Several consequences deserve to be spelled out.

    • Although ℋ was built from the eigenfunctions of 𝐿𝐾 , which depend on the choice of the measure 𝑑𝜈(𝑥),
      we know by uniqueness of the RKHS of a given kernel that ℋ itself is independent of 𝜈 and of 𝐿𝐾 . Only
      the coordinate system changes with 𝜈 .
    • Mercer’s theorem thus provides a concrete recipe for building the RKHS: take linear combinations of the
      eigenfunctions of 𝐿𝐾 , with adequately decaying weights.

    • The eigenfunctions (𝜓𝑖 )𝑖∈ℕ form an orthogonal basis of the RKHS, with

                                                                                            1
                                               ⟨𝜓𝑖 , 𝜓𝑗 ⟩ℋ = 0 for 𝑖 ≠ 𝑗,       ‖𝜓𝑖 ‖ℋ =       .
                                                                                           √𝜆𝑖
        Directions with small eigenvalues are expensive: representing a unit of 𝜓𝑖 costs 1/√𝜆𝑖 in RKHS norm.

    • Summarizing the picture that has emerged: the unit ball of ℋ , seen inside 𝐿2𝜈 (𝒳 ), is a well-defined ellipsoid
      whose principal axes are the eigenfunctions 𝜓𝑘 , with semi-axis lengths √𝜆𝑘 . A rapidly decaying spectrum
      means a thin, strongly anisotropic ellipsoid: the kernel deems only a few directions cheap, and that is exactly
      what regularization exploits.

   The spectrum therefore answers how quickly usable directions disappear and how many remain active at a
regularization scale. The atlas contrasts three canonical regimes: exact finite rank, polynomial Matérn/Sobolev
decay, and faster Gaussian decay. Their effective-dimension curves translate those approximation geometries into
statistical capacity.

Figure 16.1: Three Mercer regimes imply three capacity laws. Finite rank saturates at a fixed dimension, polynomial
Matérn/Sobolev decay retains a long tail, and the faster Gaussian spectrum activates substantially fewer directions at the
same regularization level.

   It is worth pausing on why this reweighting deserves to be called a smoothness measure, since that closes
the circle with the Green functions of the first section. In every example of the chapter the eigenfunctions 𝜓𝑘
grow more oscillatory as 𝑘 increases, sines and cosines of rising frequency on the interval, spherical harmonics of
rising degree on the sphere, while the eigenvalues 𝜆𝑘 decrease. The RKHS norm ∑𝑘 𝑎𝑘2 /𝜆𝑘 therefore multiplies
the energy 𝑎𝑘2 that a function places on the 𝑘 -th oscillation by the large weight 1/𝜆𝑘 : a function pays little for its
slow components and dearly for its fast ones, so a small RKHS norm forces the fast components to be small, which
is exactly what it means to be smooth. The rate at which 𝜆𝑘 → 0 fixes the exchange rate between frequency and
cost, and hence how strongly the norm insists on smoothness. A slowly decaying spectrum barely penalizes high
frequencies and admits rough functions; a fast decay penalizes them heavily and admits only very smooth ones.
This is the quantitative content of the slogan that opened the chapter, that choosing a kernel means choosing
which functions the norm considers simple.

16.6.2 Example: Sobolev spaces of periodic functions
Applied to the Bernoulli kernels of the first worked example, the construction identifies the RKHS as a classical
Sobolev space.

Proof sketch. The characterization by Fourier coefficients is a direct application of the RKHS construction theo-

   This closes the loop opened at the start of the chapter: smoothness penalties are RKHS norms (Green func-
tions), and RKHS norms are weighted spectral norms (Mercer). The kernel’s spectrum is a complete dial for the
smoothness the method enforces. We now show that the same dial controls statistical performance.

16.7.7 Optimality and adaptivity
     • The same rates hold for the exact quantities 𝐵𝜆 + 𝑉𝜆 , without the substitution Φ⊤    𝑛 Φ𝑛 = 𝑛𝑇 ; see Dicker
       et al. (2015, Corollaries 1 to 4), whose proof we followed and adapted. The constants hidden in the big-𝑂
       notation depend only on the kernel 𝐾 and the measure 𝑑𝜈(𝑥).
     • These rates are minimax optimal (Caponnetto and De Vito, 2007): no estimator can uniformly improve on
       them over the corresponding classes of target functions.
     • The polynomial case connects back to classical nonparametric statistics. For 𝑠 = 2𝑞 , the ball of the RKHS
       sits inside 𝐿2𝜈 (𝒳 ) as a Sobolev-type class of functions that are 𝑞 − 1 times differentiable with absolutely
       continuous derivatives and ‖𝑓 (𝑞) ‖𝐿2𝜈 (𝒳 ) < +∞, as the periodic Sobolev example made explicit with eigen-
                                                           𝑠        − 2𝑞
       values 𝑛−2𝛽 and 𝑞 = 𝛽 . The rate 𝑛− 𝑠+1 = 𝑛 2𝑞+1 is then exactly the standard optimal convergence rate of
       nonparametric regression (Tsybakov, 2009).
     • The rate depends not only on the spectrum but on how smooth the target 𝑓 ∗ is relative to the kernel. This
       is made precise by a source condition: one assumes 𝑓 ∗ = 𝑇 𝑟 𝑔 for some 𝑔 ∈ 𝐿2𝜈 (𝒳 ) and an exponent
       𝑟 > 0, where 𝑇 is the integral operator. A larger 𝑟 means 𝑓 ∗ lives deeper inside the range of 𝑇 , hence its
       coordinates 𝛽𝑖∗ decay faster relative to 𝜆𝑖 , and the achievable rate improves accordingly; the case treated
       above corresponds to 𝑟 = 12 , for which 𝑓 ∗ ∈ ℋ . The source-condition exponent and the eigenvalue-decay
       exponent together fix the minimax rate (Caponnetto and De Vito, 2007).
     • Under additional assumptions on 𝑓 ∗ , for instance requiring not only ∑𝑖≥1 (𝛽𝑖∗ )2 < ∞ but also
        ∑𝑖≥1 𝑖𝜏 (𝛽𝑖∗ )2 < ∞ for some 𝜏 > 0, or 𝛽𝑖∗ = 0 for 𝑖 > 𝐽 , one obtains faster convergence rates,
        which are again minimax optimal for the class of functions considered. In this sense KRR is adaptive:
        the same estimator, with a properly tuned 𝜆, achieves the optimal rate over a range of regularity classes
        (Caponnetto and De Vito, 2007; Dicker et al., 2015).


16.8 The integral-operator minimax framework: source and capacity
The rates corollary tied the speed of learning to a single number, the eigenvalue-decay exponent, under the stand-
ing assumption 𝑓 ∗ ∈ ℋ . That assumption quietly hides a second dial. Two targets can both lie in ℋ yet be
learnable at very different speeds, because what governs the bias is not merely that 𝑓 ∗ has finite RKHS norm but
how deep inside the smoothing action of the kernel it sits. The modern account, the integral-operator approach
to minimax learning rates, separates these two effects cleanly: a source condition measures the smoothness of the
target relative to the kernel, a capacity condition measures the richness of the kernel through its spectrum, and
a single exponent formula built from the two governs the optimal rate. The error-estimate technique was devel-
oped by Smale and Zhou (2007), and its optimal-rate form is due to Caponnetto and De Vito (2007); the framework
has since been sharpened by Steinwart, Hush, and Scovel (2009), Fischer and Steinwart (2020), and Blanchard
and Mücke (2018). This section names the framework, states its central theorem, and reads off the saturation
phenomenon that specifically limits kernel ridge regression. Both conditions are phrased through the integral
operator 𝑇 = 𝐿𝐾 , diagonal in the eigenbasis with 𝑇 𝜓𝑖 = 𝜆𝑖 𝜓𝑖 , and its spectral powers 𝑇 𝑟 ( ∑𝑖 𝑐𝑖 𝜓𝑖 ) = ∑𝑖 𝜆𝑖𝑟 𝑐𝑖 𝜓𝑖 .
282                                                                                        16 Mercer’s Theorem, Spectra, and Rates



16.8.1 The source condition
How smooth is the target relative to the kernel? The chapter’s RKHS is the range of 𝑇 1/2 , the functions whose
coordinates decay one half-power of the spectrum faster than square-summable. Demanding that 𝑓 ∗ sit even
deeper inside the range of 𝑇 , in the range of a higher power 𝑇 𝑟 , is exactly a quantitative smoothness assumption,
and it is the hypothesis under which fast rates are proved.

Definition 16.33 (source condition). The target 𝑓 ∗ satisfies a source condition of order 𝑟 > 0 with radius 𝑅 if it
lies in the range of the 𝑟 -th power of the integral operator,

                                             𝑓 ∗ = 𝑇 𝑟 𝑔,     ‖𝑔‖𝐿2𝜈 (𝒳 ) ≤ 𝑅,
   where 𝑇 𝑟 is defined by the spectral calculus. Equivalently, writing 𝑓 ∗ = ∑𝑖 𝑐𝑖 𝜓𝑖 in the 𝐿2𝜈 eigenbasis, the coor-
dinates obey

                                                          𝑐𝑖2     2
                                                      ∑
                                                          𝜆 2𝑟 ≤ 𝑅 .
                                                      𝑖≥1  𝑖
   The larger the exponent 𝑟 , the faster the coordinates 𝑐𝑖 must decay relative to 𝜆𝑖𝑟 , so the deeper 𝑓 ∗ sits inside the
smoothed range of 𝑇 and the smoother it is relative to the kernel. The threshold 𝑟 = 12 is precisely membership
in the RKHS: since ‖𝑓 ∗ ‖2ℋ = ∑𝑖 𝑐𝑖2 /𝜆𝑖 , the source condition at 𝑟 = 12 reads ∑𝑖 𝑐𝑖2 /𝜆𝑖 ≤ 𝑅2 , that is, 𝑓 ∗ ∈ ℋ
with ‖𝑓 ∗ ‖ℋ ≤ 𝑅. So 𝑟 = 12 recovers exactly the standing hypothesis of the rate analysis above, as the optimality
remarks already anticipated; 𝑟 > 12 asks for a genuinely smoother target, while 𝑟 ∈ (0, 12 ) admits targets rougher
than a generic RKHS element, the misspecified regime handled by Steinwart, Hush, and Scovel (2009) and by
Fischer and Steinwart (2020) through an additional embedding condition on the eigenfunctions.

16.8.2 The capacity condition and the effective dimension
The source condition speaks about the target; the second dial speaks about the kernel and the space it lives on. It
asks how many directions the estimator is forced to fit, and the right measure is the effective dimension already
met in the variance analysis, now promoted to a hypothesis in its own right.

Definition 16.34 (capacity condition). The kernel satisfies a capacity condition with exponent 𝑝 ∈ (0, 1] if the
effective dimension

                                                                              𝜆𝑖
                                        𝑁 (𝜆) = tr(𝑇 (𝑇 + 𝜆𝐼 )−1 ) = ∑
                                                                       𝑖≥1 𝜆𝑖 + 𝜆
      obeys 𝑁 (𝜆) ≤ 𝐶 𝜆−𝑝 for all 𝜆 > 0 and some constant 𝐶 .
   A polynomially decaying spectrum 𝜆𝑖 ≍ 𝑖−1/𝑝 , equivalently 𝜆𝑖 ≍ 𝑖−𝑠 with 𝑠 = 1/𝑝 , gives exactly 𝑁 (𝜆) ≍ 𝜆−𝑝 .
The borderline 𝑝 = 1 is nothing more than the trace-class bound ∑𝑖 𝜆𝑖 < ∞ proved for every Mercer kernel, which
always yields 𝑁 (𝜆) ≤ 𝜆−1 ∑𝑖 𝜆𝑖 ; a smaller 𝑝 means a faster-decaying spectrum, a smaller effective dimension,
and therefore fewer directions carrying variance. This is the same reading as the effective-dimension remark of
the Mercer section: 𝑁 (𝜆) counts, softly, the eigenvalues above the threshold 𝜆, and the capacity exponent 𝑝 is
the growth rate of that count as 𝜆 → 0. It is this exponent, not the ambient dimension, that fixes the size of the
variance.

16.8.3 The minimax rate and the saturation of KRR
With both dials in place the optimal rate is a single closed expression in the two exponents.

Theorem 16.35 (Caponnetto and De Vito, 2007). Suppose the kernel satisfies the capacity condition with exponent
𝑝 ∈ (0, 1] and the target the source condition with exponent 𝑟 ∈ [ 12 , 1] and radius 𝑅. Then kernel ridge regression
with regularization 𝜆𝑛 ≍ 𝑛−1/(2𝑟+𝑝) has excess risk
16.8 The integral-operator minimax framework: source and capacity                                                                        283




                                                                    2                          − 2𝑟
                                                𝔼 ‖𝑓𝜆̂ 𝑛 − 𝑓 ∗ ‖ 2            ≤ 𝐶 (𝑅2 + 𝜎 2 ) 𝑛 2𝑟+𝑝 ,
                                                                    𝐿𝜈 (𝒳 )
                      2𝑟
   and the exponent 2𝑟+𝑝  is minimax optimal: no estimator attains a uniformly faster rate over the class of distribu-
tions meeting these two conditions.
   Assumptions. All domains, quantifiers, regularity conditions, and parameter restrictions stated in the result are in force; no converse is
implied. Proof status. No separate proof is attached to this result; independent technical review must determine whether the surrounding
derivation is sufficient.

  The formula reproduces every rate of the corollary above as a special case. At 𝑟 = 12 , the case 𝑓 ∗ ∈ ℋ , and
                                                             2𝑟     1     𝑠
capacity 𝑝 = 1/𝑠 from a spectrum 𝜆𝑖 ≍ 𝑖−𝑠 , the exponent is 2𝑟+𝑝 = 1+𝑝 = 𝑠+1 , exactly the polynomial-decay rate
𝑛−𝑠/(𝑠+1) obtained earlier by hand. The framework only makes explicit what the hand computation left implicit,
that the rate also depends on the smoothness of the target, and it is the product structure 2𝑟/(2𝑟 + 𝑝) that shows
how the two dependencies interlock.
   The intuition is exactly the bias-variance split already computed, now read through the operator calculus. The
kernel ridge estimator smooths the target by 𝑔𝜆 (𝑇 ) = (𝑇 + 𝜆𝐼 )−1 , so its bias is the smoothing residual applied to
𝑓 ∗,
                                                                                                                    𝜆𝑡𝑟
                      bias(𝜆) = ‖𝜆(𝑇 + 𝜆𝐼 )−1 𝑓 ∗ ‖ 2                   = ‖𝜆(𝑇 + 𝜆𝐼 )−1 𝑇 𝑟 𝑔‖ 2        ≤ ( sup          ) 𝑅.
                                                                                                          0≤𝑡≤‖𝑇 ‖ 𝑡 + 𝜆
                                                           𝐿𝜈 (𝒳 )                            𝐿𝜈 (𝒳 )

   For 0 < 𝑟 ≤ 1 the scalar supremum is of order 𝜆𝑟 , attained near 𝑡 ≍ 𝜆, so bias(𝜆)2 ≲ 𝜆2𝑟 𝑅2 : a larger source
exponent shrinks the bias faster as 𝜆 → 0. The variance is controlled by capacity, since the spectral bound of the
previous section reads 𝑉̃𝜆 ≲ 𝜎 2 𝑁 (𝜆)/𝑛 ≲ 𝜎 2 𝜆−𝑝 /𝑛. Balancing the two,

                                           𝜆−𝑝         − 1                                                  − 2𝑟
                                  𝜆2𝑟 ≍        ⟹ 𝜆𝑛 ≍ 𝑛 2𝑟+𝑝 ,                      bias2 + variance ≍ 𝑛 2𝑟+𝑝 .
                                            𝑛
   The source exponent governs how fast the bias falls, the capacity exponent how slowly the variance rises, and
the rate is the crossing point of the two.

Remark 16.36 (saturation of KRR at 𝑟 = 1). The bias estimate conceals a ceiling. The scalar function 𝑡 ↦
𝜆 𝑡 𝑟 /(𝑡 + 𝜆) has order 𝜆𝑟 only while 𝑟 ≤ 1; for 𝑟 > 1 its supremum over 𝑡 ∈ [0, ‖𝑇 ‖] is attained at the top of the
spectrum and has order 𝜆, not 𝜆𝑟 . The kernel ridge bias therefore saturates: bias(𝜆)2 ≍ 𝜆2 for every 𝑟 ≥ 1, so the
best achievable rate freezes at 𝑛−2/(2+𝑝) , the value already reached at 𝑟 = 1, no matter how much smoother 𝑓 ∗
is. The minimax rate 𝑛−2𝑟/(2𝑟+𝑝) keeps improving past 𝑟 = 1, so on very smooth targets plain kernel ridge regres-
sion is provably suboptimal. Recovering the faster rate requires a higher-qualification spectral regularizer, such
as iterated Tikhonov, spectral cut-off, or gradient-flow (Landweber) learning, analyzed in one inverse-problems
framework by Blanchard and Mücke (2018). The gap between the two exponents past 𝑟 = 1 is the price of the
simplest regularizer.
  The whole mechanism is easiest to trust in numbers: a concrete spectrum, its measured effective dimension,
and the rate exponent seen to plateau in the source exponent.

Example 16.37 (effective dimension, rate exponent, and saturation). Setup.
   Take the polynomial spectrum 𝜆𝑖 = 𝑖−2𝑏 of the integral operator 𝑇 with 𝑏 = 1, that is 𝜆𝑖 = 𝑖−2 , so the decay
exponent is 𝑠 = 2𝑏 = 2. The theory predicts capacity exponent 𝑝 = 1/(2𝑏) = 12 . We read off the effective
dimension, the predicted kernel ridge rate exponent as a function of the source exponent 𝑟 , and the saturation at
𝑟 = 1. The noise level 𝜎 2 enters only through constants.
    1. Confirm trace class. The eigenvalues sum to ∑𝑖≥1 𝑖−2 = 1.644934, the value 𝜋 2 /6, which is finite, so 𝑇
       is trace class and the analysis applies. The capacity exponent 𝑝 = 1 would already follow from this bound
       alone; the point is to do better.
    2. Compute the effective dimension. Summing 𝑁 (𝜆) = ∑𝑖 𝜆𝑖 /(𝜆𝑖 + 𝜆) at three scales,
284                                                                                                   16 Mercer’s Theorem, Spectra, and Rates




                               𝑁 (10−2 ) = 15.208,           𝑁 (10−3 ) = 49.173,          𝑁 (10−4 ) = 156.580,

         each within half a unit of the asymptote (𝜋/2) 𝜆−1/2 , namely 15.708, 49.673, 157.080. A log-log fit of
         𝑁 (𝜆) across 𝜆 ∈ [10−2 , 10−6 ] has slope −0.5032, so the measured capacity exponent is 𝑝 ≈ 0.50, matching
         1/(2𝑏).
      3. Read the rate exponent. With 𝑝 = 12 , the kernel ridge exponent 𝜌KRR (𝑟) = 2 min(𝑟, 1)/ (2 min(𝑟, 1) + 𝑝)
         and the minimax exponent 𝜌min (𝑟) = 2𝑟/(2𝑟 + 𝑝) are

                                                      𝑟        𝜌KRR (𝑟)     𝜌min (𝑟)
                                                      0.5      0.6667       0.6667
                                                      0.75     0.7500       0.7500
                                                      1.0      0.8000       0.8000
                                                      1.5      0.8000       0.8571
                                                      2.0      0.8000       0.8889
                                                      3.0      0.8000       0.9231


         At 𝑟 = 12 this reproduces the chapter’s polynomial rate 𝑛−𝑠/(𝑠+1) = 𝑛−2/3 for 𝑓 ∗ ∈ ℋ . The two columns
         agree up to 𝑟 = 1, then 𝜌KRR sticks at 2/(2 + 𝑝) = 0.8 while 𝜌min keeps climbing.

      4. See the saturation in the balance. At 𝑛 = 104 , tuning 𝜆∗ = 𝑛−1/(2 min(𝑟,1)+𝑝) and reading bias2 =
         𝜆∗2 min(𝑟,1) and variance = 𝑁 (𝜆∗ )/𝑛: for 𝑟 = 12 , 𝜆∗ = 2.154 × 10−3 , bias2 = 2.154 × 10−3 , variance =
         3.334 × 10−3 ; for 𝑟 = 1, 𝜆∗ = 2.512 × 10−2 , bias2 = 6.310 × 10−4 , variance = 9.411 × 10−4 . The 𝑟 = 2
         target produces the same three numbers as 𝑟 = 1, to every printed digit: kernel ridge regression cannot tell
         a twice-smoother target from a once-smoother one.

   Reading. Two exponents, not one, set the rate: the capacity 𝑝 = 12 , fixed by the spectrum, and the source 𝑟 , fixed
by the target. They combine as 2 min(𝑟, 1)/ (2 min(𝑟, 1) + 𝑝), and the min(𝑟, 1) is the fingerprint of saturation.
Past 𝑟 = 1 the kernel ridge estimator leaves speed on the table that a higher-qualification method would collect.

16.9 Beyond compactness: an outlook
Everything in this chapter leaned on two hypotheses: 𝒳 compact and 𝐾 continuous. Suppose now that 𝒳 is not
compact, for example 𝒳 = ℝ𝑑 . Then the eigenvalue problem ∫ 𝐾 (𝑥, 𝑡) 𝜓 (𝑡) 𝑑𝜈(𝑡) = 𝜆 𝜓 (𝑥) need not have a
                                                                     𝒳
countable family of eigenvalues, and Mercer’s theorem does not hold. For the most important class of kernels on
ℝ𝑑 , the translation invariant (or shift-invariant) kernels 𝐾 (𝑥, 𝑦) = 𝜑(𝑥 − 𝑦), Fourier transforms provide a conve-
nient extension, and harmonic analysis brings kernels well beyond vector spaces, to groups and semigroups.
   The simplest instance already displays the whole mechanism. Call a kernel 𝐾 ∶ ℤ × ℤ → ℝ translation
invariant (or shift-invariant) if it depends only on the difference of its arguments, 𝐾 (𝑥, 𝑦) = 𝑎𝑥−𝑦 for some
sequence (𝑎𝑛 )𝑛∈ℤ , the sequence being called positive definite when the kernel is. A classical theorem of Herglotz
states that a sequence (𝑎𝑛 )𝑛∈ℤ is positive definite if and only if it is the Fourier-Stieltjes transform of a positive
measure 𝜇 ∈ 𝑀(𝕋), the set of finite Borel measures on the torus [0, 2𝜋] with 0 and 2𝜋 identified. The countable
spectrum of eigenvalues has become a spectral measure. The next chapter develops this theme: Herglotz on ℤ,
Bochner’s theorem on ℝ𝑑 , the RKHS of shift-invariant kernels, and the generalization to semigroups.

Remark 16.38 (Further reading). The spectral picture of this chapter is developed at book length in two standard
references. Schölkopf and Smola (2002), Learning with Kernels, treat Mercer’s theorem, the integral operator, and
the eigenfunction feature map in their Chapter 2, with the functional-analytic prerequisites, the spectral theo-
rem, and the proof of Mercer’s expansion collected in the mathematical appendix; their exposition is the natural
complement to the operator vocabulary introduced here. Shawe-Taylor and Cristianini (2004), Kernel Methods
16.10 Common mistakes and practical implications                                                                   285



for Pattern Analysis, cover the same ground from the properties-of-kernels angle in their Chapter 3, including
Mercer’s theorem and the eigen-decomposition of the Gram matrix as the finite shadow of the integral operator,
and they are especially good on the data-driven, empirical version of the spectrum that our figure previews.
   For the statistical half of the chapter, the convergence rates of kernel ridge regression, the comprehensive
reference is Steinwart and Christmann (2008), Support Vector Machines, whose treatment of integral operators,
effective dimension, and the interplay between eigenvalue decay and learning rates places the results of the final
section in their full generality. The reader who wants the sharpest and most complete rate theory should read it
alongside the primary sources cited in the text, Cucker and Smale (2002), Caponnetto and De Vito (2007), Bach
(2013), and Tsybakov (2009).


16.10 Common mistakes and practical implications
    • Keep the measure 𝜈 visible. Mercer eigenfunctions and eigenvalues depend on it even though the RKHS
      determined by 𝐾 does not.
    • Do not divide by a zero eigenvalue. The RKHS contains only coefficients supported on positive-eigenvalue
      directions.
    • Distinguish exact risk identities from the approximation Φ⊤
                                                                𝑛 Φ𝑛 ≈ 𝑛𝑇 ; the latter explains rates but is not an
      equality for a finite random sample.
    • Compare spectra only after fixing kernel scaling, domain, and sampling measure. Eigenvalue decay is not
      a property of a kernel formula in isolation.
    • Tune 𝜆 to both capacity and target smoothness. Faster kernel eigenvalue decay lowers variance but may
      make a rough target expensive to approximate.


16.11 Summary and further reading
Mercer’s theorem turns a continuous positive-definite kernel on a compact measured space into an orthogonal
spectrum. That spectrum constructs the RKHS, where a coefficient in direction 𝜓𝑖 costs 1/𝜆𝑖 , and it also controls
learning, where 𝜆𝑖 /(𝜆𝑖 + 𝜆) counts how active the same direction remains. Polynomial, exponential, and finite-
rank spectra therefore produce different effective dimensions and different bias-variance balances. Source condi-
tions add the missing target-side coordinate: capacity describes what the kernel offers, while source smoothness
describes how the truth occupies it. For foundational and extended treatments, see (Mercer 1909), (Aronszajn
1950), (Caponnetto and De Vito 2007), and (Steinwart and Scovel 2009).

CHAPTER 17




Inverse Learning and Spectral
Regularization

        Why does stopping gradient descent early prevent overfitting, and why can an interrupted opti-
     mizer behave like a ridge penalty? Kernel regression is an inverse problem in disguise. The popu-
     lation operator suppresses directions with small eigenvalues, while estimation tries to reconstruct
     them from noisy samples. Direct inversion divides by those eigenvalues and can turn a harmless
     perturbation into the largest component of the answer. Ridge, spectral cutoff, Landweber iteration,
     and conjugate gradients all decide how much of each direction may pass. Their spectral filters make
     that decision visible. Source conditions describe the target, effective dimension describes the num-
     ber of noisy directions available to the estimator, and qualification describes the smoothness a filter
     can exploit before it saturates. This chapter develops those claims from their operator assumptions
     through rate calculations, stopping rules, failure witnesses, and a worked spectral audit.




17.1 The two inverse problems hidden in regression
Let (𝒳 , 𝒜 , 𝑃𝑋 ) be a probability space and let ℋ be a separable real RKHS with measurable kernel 𝑘 . Assume

                                                sup 𝑘(𝑥, 𝑥) ≤ 𝜅 2 < ∞.

17.1.1 Paper module: Rosasco et al. make the analogy literal
Before (Rosasco et al. 2004), regularized learning and inverse problems had similar formulas, but the direct oper-
ator and the stochastic analogue of observation noise were often left implicit. Their move was to take the RKHS
inclusion 𝑆 as the forward operator and the empirical sampling map 𝑆𝑛 as its random discretization. This turns
regularized least squares into Tikhonov regularization of a perturbed normal equation.
   The exact setting in their Sections 4 and 5 uses a continuous bounded kernel, square loss, bounded responses,
and i.i.d. sampling. The stochastic perturbations are

                                      𝛿1,𝑛 = ‖𝑔𝑛 − 𝑆 ∗ 𝑓𝜌 ‖ℋ ,      𝛿2,𝑛 = ‖𝑇𝑛 − 𝑇 ‖ℒ (ℋ ) .
   The contribution is not the formula for ridge. It is the decomposition of learning error into a deterministic
regularization argument, expressed in (𝛿1,𝑛 , 𝛿2,𝑛 , 𝜆), followed by a probabilistic control of the two perturbations.
This separates the functional-analytic question from concentration.
   For the empirical Tikhonov estimator

                                                      𝑓̂𝜆 = (𝑇𝑛 + 𝜆𝐼 )−1 𝑔𝑛 ,
      the resolvent identity gives

                                𝑓̂𝜆 − 𝑓𝜆 = (𝑇𝑛 + 𝜆𝐼 )−1 (𝑔𝑛 − 𝑔) + (𝑇𝑛 + 𝜆𝐼 )−1 (𝑇 − 𝑇𝑛 )𝑓𝜆 ,
      where 𝑔 = 𝑆 ∗ 𝑓𝜌 and 𝑓𝜆 = (𝑇 + 𝜆𝐼 )−1 𝑔 . Since ‖(𝑇𝑛 + 𝜆𝐼 )−1 ‖ ≤ 𝜆−1 ,

                                                         𝛿1,𝑛 + 𝛿2,𝑛 ‖𝑓𝜆 ‖ℋ
                                               ‖𝑓̂𝜆 − 𝑓𝜆 ‖ℋ ≤               .
                                                                 𝜆
   This bound is deliberately crude, but it exposes the mechanism: 𝜆 must tend to zero to remove approximation
bias, yet not so quickly that empirical perturbations divided by 𝜆 explode.
   Failure boundary. The construction does not identify components in ker 𝑆 , does not cover arbitrary losses
without a different nonlinear operator, and does not make the inverse bounded. Regularization selects a stable
approximation; it cannot recover information absent from the range of the forward operator.

17.3 Source conditions, qualification, and saturation

can continue converting larger 𝜈 into faster bias decay, whereas first-order Tikhonov regularization cannot exploit
smoothness beyond qualification one. The plate isolates this bias mechanism; variance and parameter choice
must be added before it becomes a risk comparison.

17.4 Paper module: source, capacity, and minimax rates
Caponnetto and De Vito asked when regularized least squares attains a rate that no learning algorithm can uni-
formly improve over the same model class (Caponnetto and De Vito 2007). Their key advance was to couple a
source condition with eigenvalue decay instead of describing complexity only by a global RKHS radius.
   Their exact scalar specialization assumes a separable RKHS with uniformly bounded evaluation, i.i.d. obser-
vations, a Bernstein-type moment condition on 𝑌 − 𝑓ℋ (𝑋 ), and existence of a minimum-norm risk minimizer.

capacity, and the moment condition controls stochastic fluctuations.

17.5 Interpolation spaces and misspecification
The power spaces of 𝐿 = 𝑆𝑆 ∗ express target regularity even when the target is not an RKHS element.

Definition 17.5 (power space). For 𝜃 ≥ 0, define


                                    [ℋ ]𝜃 = ran 𝐿𝜃/2 = {∑ 𝑎𝑗 𝜇𝑗𝜃/2 𝜓𝑗 ∶ ∑ 𝑎𝑗2 < ∞} ,
                                                              𝑗                  𝑗
      with the minimum-preimage norm and with the null space of 𝐿 factored out.
   The endpoint 𝜃 = 0 is the closure of the positive eigenspace in 𝐿2 (𝑃𝑋 ), while 𝜃 = 1 is the embedded RKHS. Un-
der the compact-embedding assumptions made explicit in (Steinwart and Scovel 2012), intermediate 𝜃 describes
interpolation between them. The identification depends on both kernel and measure. It must not be replaced by
an unqualified statement such as “a Matérn RKHS is a Sobolev space” on an arbitrary domain.
   Misspecified regression often places 𝑓𝜌 in [ℋ ]𝜃 with 𝜃 < 1. Then the target can be approximated in prediction
norm even though no finite RKHS norm exists. Bounds in ℋ -norm may be meaningless while 𝐿2 (𝑃𝑋 ) bounds
remain valid.

                                                𝑛 𝑗                 𝑛 𝑗

   which is the empirical complexity evaluated at (𝜂𝑡)−1/2 . The stopping rule is therefore a computable bias-
variance balance, not an analogy to ridge.
   Failure boundary. The theorem does not license arbitrary adaptive optimizers, arbitrary initialization,
unknown-noise substitution, classification losses, or unrestricted multiple passes of stochastic gradient descent.
Its empirical-norm theorem is conditional on the design. The random-design conclusion needs an additional
comparison between empirical and population complexity.

A useful example should report both prediction and instability. Consider a normalized empirical operator with

   Interpolation wins this one low-noise prediction comparison, yet its inverse norm is ten to nineteen times

alone does not identify the best predictor.

17.8 Parameter choice, Krylov methods, and computation
The regularization path is incomplete until its selection rule is specified.

       • A discrepancy principle uses a known or independently estimated noise scale.
       • Cross-validation estimates prediction risk but must respect dependence and preprocessing.
       • Generalized cross-validation uses the trace of a linear smoother and can fail under leverage heterogeneity.
       • Lepskiĭ-type rules compare scales and require a stochastic envelope.
       • Marginal likelihood selects a variance ratio under a probabilistic model, not an arbitrary downstream loss.

      Conjugate gradients add another complication. At step 𝑡 , the estimate lies in

                                              𝒦𝑡 (𝑇𝑛 , 𝑔𝑛 ) = span{𝑔𝑛 , 𝑇𝑛 𝑔𝑛 , … , 𝑇𝑛𝑡−1 𝑔𝑛 }.
   Its residual polynomial is data dependent. Fast reduction of the linear-system residual does not imply stable
reconstruction, because the polynomial can begin resolving noisy weak directions. Preconditioning changes both
the Krylov space and the implicit regularizer. It must be reported as part of the estimator.

Algorithm 17.8 (auditable spectral-regularizer comparison).       1. Fix the normalization of 𝐾 , the prediction
     norm, and the source of the noise estimate.
  2. Estimate spectral bounds and verify positive self-adjoint matrix products.
  3. Run ridge, cutoff, Landweber, and conjugate-gradient paths at matched kernel-product budgets.
  4. Record prediction residual, validation loss, solution norm, effective degrees of freedom, and inverse ampli-
     fication.
  5. Apply the stopping or selection rule without test reuse.
  6. Perturb observations at the declared noise scale and rerun the selected estimator.
  7. Report preconditioner, precision, jitter, convergence threshold, and whether the rule or compute budget
     stopped the solve.
   Stochastic gradients require a separate analysis. Mini-batch size, sampling scheme, averaging, and number of
passes jointly determine the estimator. There may be no deterministic scalar filter. Calling every undertrained
stochastic optimizer “spectral regularization” hides this distinction.

   The same framework appears in conditional mean operators, instrumental-variable equations, vector-valued
regression, deconvolution, and scientific inverse problems. In each case, the operator, its range, the norm of in-
terest, and the source condition must be retyped. A regularized solution outside the identifiable range is not
recovered truth.


17.10 Common mistakes and practical implications
    • 𝑆 ∗ 𝑆 and 𝑆𝑆 ∗ have related spectra but act on different spaces.
    • The empirical problem perturbs the operator and the right-hand side.
    • Source conditions are relative to 𝑇 , not universal smoothness labels.
    • Qualification limits exploitable source regularity.
    • Effective dimension controls a variance scale, not numerical conditioning by itself.
    • Early stopping includes initialization, step sizes, and the stopping rule.
    • A small residual can coexist with an unstable inverse.
    • A minimax exponent is meaningful only with its model class and norm.
    • Finite precision adds an implicit cutoff that can dominate the mathematical filter.


17.11 Summary and further reading
Inverse learning begins with a typed operator equation. Spectral filters stabilize it by replacing division by 𝜇 with a
controlled function 𝑔𝜆 (𝜇). Rosasco et al. identify sampling as random operator discretization (Rosasco et al. 2004).
Caponnetto and De Vito couple source and capacity assumptions to obtain matching rate exponents (Caponnetto
and De Vito 2007). Raskutti et al. derive a computable early-stopping rule from empirical eigenvalues and local
complexity (Raskutti et al. 2014). The transferable lesson is not that every method is secretly ridge. It is that bias,
stochastic variance, qualification, identifiability, and numerical stability must be audited in the same spectral
coordinates.

CHAPTER 18




Kernel Interpolation and
Approximation Theory

     A network of weather stations reports temperature at a few hundred scattered sites, and a fore-
   caster must fill in the map between them; a wind-tunnel campaign yields drag at a dozen operating
   points, and an engineer must predict it everywhere else. Both want a surface that passes exactly
   through the measurements, together with an honest statement of how wrong it can be in between.
   Machine learning instinct says exact fitting is overfitting, yet approximation theory reaches the op-
   posite verdict: when the data are noiseless, the kernel interpolant is the optimal recovery of every
   function the kernel’s norm can measure, and it comes with a computable pointwise error bar. This
   chapter builds that theory. We solve the interpolation system and prove the solution has minimum
   RKHS norm, read the native space as a smoothness scale through the Fourier transform, derive
   the power function and recognize it as the Gaussian-process posterior standard deviation, convert
   point-set geometry into convergence rates, and prove the uncertainty relation that couples spectral
   accuracy to exponential ill-conditioning.




18.1 Kernel interpolation as minimum-norm recovery
Suppose we observe a function exactly, with no noise, at finitely many sites. What should we do with a kernel
then? The regularized machinery of Chapter 4, Kernel Ridge Regression and Smooth Losses was built to trade
data fit against smoothness, but with exact data there is nothing to trade: we should fit the observations exactly
and let the RKHS norm arbitrate among the infinitely many functions that do.

Definition 18.1 (kernel interpolation problem). Let 𝑘 be a strictly positive definite kernel on 𝒳 with RKHS ℋ𝑘 ,
let 𝑋 = {𝑥1 , … , 𝑥𝑛 } ⊂ 𝒳 be distinct sites, and let 𝑦1 , … , 𝑦𝑛 be target values. The kernel interpolant is
                                                 𝑛
                                        𝑠(𝑥) = ∑ 𝑐𝑗 𝑘(𝑥, 𝑥𝑗 ),      𝐾 𝑐 = 𝑦,
                                                𝑗=1

   where 𝐾 = [𝑘(𝑥𝑖 , 𝑥𝑗 )]𝑛𝑖,𝑗=1 is the Gram matrix. Strict positive definiteness and distinctness of the sites make 𝐾
invertible, so 𝑐 = 𝐾 −1 𝑦 exists and is unique, and 𝑠(𝑥𝑖 ) = 𝑦𝑖 for every 𝑖.
300                                                                                                   18 Kernel Interpolation and Approximation Theory



  The ansatz 𝑠 ∈ span{𝑘(⋅, 𝑥𝑗 )} is not a convenience; it is forced by optimality. Among all functions in ℋ𝑘 that
pass through the data, the interpolant is the one the norm likes best.

Proposition 18.2 (minimum-norm interpolation). Let 𝑠 = ∑𝑗 𝑐𝑗 𝑘(⋅, 𝑥𝑗 ) with 𝐾 𝑐 = 𝑦 be the kernel interpolant of
the data. Then for every 𝑔 ∈ ℋ𝑘 with 𝑔(𝑥𝑖 ) = 𝑦𝑖 for all 𝑖,

                                                         ‖𝑔‖2ℋ𝑘 = ‖𝑠‖2ℋ𝑘 + ‖𝑔 − 𝑠‖2ℋ𝑘 ,
      so 𝑠 is the unique minimum-norm interpolant of the data.
      Assumptions. 𝑘 strictly positive definite, sites distinct, at least one interpolant exists in ℋ𝑘 . Proof status. complete.

Proof. Let 𝑔 interpolate the data and set 𝑢 = 𝑔 − 𝑠 . Then 𝑢(𝑥𝑖 ) = 0 for every 𝑖. By the reproducing property,

                                          ⟨𝑢, 𝑠⟩ℋ𝑘 = ⟨𝑢, ∑ 𝑐𝑗 𝑘(⋅, 𝑥𝑗 )⟩           = ∑ 𝑐𝑗 𝑢(𝑥𝑗 ) = 0,
                                                               𝑗              ℋ𝑘        𝑗

   so 𝑢 ⟂ 𝑠 and the Pythagorean identity gives ‖𝑔‖2 = ‖𝑠‖2 + ‖𝑢‖2 . The norm of any competitor strictly exceeds
‖𝑠‖ unless 𝑢 = 0, which proves uniqueness.

   Three familiar objects are special cases. First, kernel ridge regression: the ridge coefficients (𝐾 + 𝜆𝐼 )−1 𝑦 con-
verge to 𝐾 −1 𝑦 as 𝜆 → 0+ , so interpolation is noiseless ridge, the endpoint of the regularization path studied in
Chapter 4, Kernel Ridge Regression and Smooth Losses. Second, kriging: geostatisticians write the same linear
system with a covariance function in place of 𝑘 and call 𝑠 the simple kriging predictor, the reading developed in
Chapter 31, Spatial and Spatiotemporal Kernel Models. Third, splines: with the kernels of Chapter 30, Smooth-
ing Splines and Additive RKHS Models, minimum-norm interpolation is exactly natural spline interpolation, the
historical root of the whole subject (Wahba 1990). Approximation theorists arrived at this triangle from scattered-
data interpolation with radial basis functions, and their monographs (Wendland 2005; Fasshauer 2007) are the
source for most of what follows.


18.2 The native space
Whose functions does the error theory cover? Every bound in this chapter is stated for targets in the RKHS of
𝑘 , which the approximation literature calls the native space of the kernel and constructs, following (Aronszajn
1950), as the completion of finite kernel combinations. The name change signals a change of viewpoint: rather
than a feature-space device, the native space is read as a concrete smoothness class, and the cleanest reading is
through the Fourier transform.

   The formula says that membership in ℋ𝑘 is a decay condition on 𝑓 ̂: the spectrum of 𝑓 must vanish at high

and Rates.

   The Gaussian kernel sits at the opposite extreme. Its Fourier transform is again a Gaussian, so membership

requires |𝑓 |̂ 2 to decay faster than 𝑒 −𝜎 ‖𝜔‖ /2 . The native space is tiny: every member extends to an analytic func-

and Christmann 2008). The cost is concrete. The error bounds of this chapter are multiplied by ‖𝑓 ‖ℋ𝑘 , and
for a target outside the native space that factor is infinite, so the bound says nothing. Gaussian interpolation
of merely Sobolev-smooth targets still works, but its analysis needs the escape results of a later section, and its
fast-convergence promises apply only to the very smooth.


18.3 The power function
An interpolant without an error estimate is a guess. The question this section answers: at a point 𝑥 where we
did not measure, how wrong can 𝑠(𝑥) be, over all targets the native space admits? The answer is the norm of the
pointwise error functional.
   Write the interpolant of data 𝑓 (𝑥1 ), … , 𝑓 (𝑥𝑛 ) in cardinal form: 𝑠𝑓 (𝑥) = 𝑘𝑋 (𝑥)⊤ 𝐾 −1 𝑦 = ∑𝑗 𝑤𝑗 (𝑥)𝑓 (𝑥𝑗 ), where
𝑘𝑋 (𝑥) = (𝑘(𝑥, 𝑥1 ), … , 𝑘(𝑥, 𝑥𝑛 ))⊤ and 𝑤(𝑥) = 𝐾 −1 𝑘𝑋 (𝑥) are weights independent of 𝑓 . The error at 𝑥 is then a
linear functional of 𝑓 ,

Proof. The error is the inner product of 𝑓 with the representer 𝑟𝑥 = 𝑘(⋅, 𝑥) − ∑𝑗 𝑤𝑗 (𝑥)𝑘(⋅, 𝑥𝑗 ), so Cauchy-Schwarz

vanish.

   The closed form deserves a second look, because we have met it before. It is precisely the posterior variance
of a noise-free Gaussian process with covariance 𝑘 conditioned on observations at 𝑋 , as derived in Chapter 49,
Gaussian Processes and the RVM. The identical formula carries two meanings: for the Bayesian it is an average-
case error bar under a prior, and for the approximation theorist it is a worst-case error bar over the unit ball of the
native space (Rasmussen and Williams 2006). The same object, integrated over the domain, became the worst-
case quadrature error of Chapter 44, Kernel Quadrature and Herding; here we meet its pointwise ancestor. We
return to this two-way reading at the end of the chapter.
   The pointwise shape matters as much as the formula. Uncertainty vanishes at every interpolation site, grows in
the gaps between sites, and becomes largest where the design leaves the domain least covered. For the minimum
kernel this geometry can be computed exactly, so the interpolant and its sharp native-space envelope can be
placed on the same axes.

  The power function converts geometry into error, so the next step is to summarize the geometry of 𝑋 in two

Definition 18.6 (fill distance and separation radius). For a site set 𝑋 ⊂ Ω ⊂ ℝ𝑑 , the fill distance and separation
radius are

                                                              ℎ𝑋 ,Ω = sup min ‖𝑥 − 𝑥𝑗 ‖,            𝑞𝑋 = 12 min‖𝑥𝑖 − 𝑥𝑗 ‖.

    𝑋 is quasi-uniform with mesh ratio 𝜌 when ℎ𝑋 ,Ω ≤ 𝜌 𝑞𝑋 .
   The fill distance is the radius of the largest data-free ball: it measures how well 𝑋 covers Ω and governs accu-
racy. The separation radius measures how close two sites come, governs stability, and appears in the next section.
Convergence theorems bound the power function by powers of ℎ.

Theorem 18.7 (fill-distance error rates). Let Ω ⊂ ℝ𝑑 be a bounded Lipschitz domain and let 𝑘 have native space
norm-equivalent to 𝐻 𝜏 (Ω) with 𝜏 > 𝑑/2, as for the Matern family. There are constants 𝐶, ℎ0 such that for all 𝑋 with
ℎ = ℎ𝑋 ,Ω ≤ ℎ0 and all 𝑓 ∈ ℋ𝑘 ,

    For the Gaussian kernel the rate is spectral: ‖𝑓 − 𝑠𝑓 ‖𝐿∞ (Ω) ≤ 𝐶𝑒 −𝑐 |log ℎ|/ℎ ‖𝑓 ‖ℋ𝑘 for some 𝑐 > 0.
  Assumptions. Bounded Lipschitz domain, ℎ below a domain-dependent threshold, target in the native space. Proof status. cited from
(Wendland 2005).

   The reading is direct: each extra order of kernel smoothness buys one extra power of ℎ, and infinitely smooth
kernels buy rates faster than any polynomial. The rates depend on 𝑋 only through ℎ, so they reward covering, not
abundance: a thousand points crowded in one corner have the same fill distance as a handful spread well. Quasi-
uniformity enters when constants must not degrade as points are added, and in the sharper results of the escape
section below; in practice near-uniform designs, or sequential designs that greedily shrink the largest power-
function value, keep 𝜌 bounded. The statistical, noisy analogue of this bias analysis, where rates are driven by
eigenvalue decay rather than fill distance, is the subject of Chapter 16, Mercer’s Theorem, Spectra, and Rates and
of (Caponnetto and De Vito 2007); the two theories describe the same estimator under different data models.


18.5 Stability and the uncertainty principle
Approximation and numerical stability can move in opposite directions. For analytic kernels on increasingly
dense sites, an error bound may fall exponentially while the Gram condition number grows exponentially. The
schematic experiment below uses explicit monotone laws to expose that conflict; it is a regime map, not a claim
that the displayed constants apply to every kernel or point set.

  Everything so far argues for the smoothest kernel available: more smoothness, faster rates. The linear algebra
objects. The system 𝐾 𝑐 = 𝑦 must be solved, and its condition number is governed by the separation radius:
304                                                                                                18 Kernel Interpolation and Approximation Theory



for a kernel of Sobolev smoothness 𝜏 , the smallest Gram eigenvalue obeys a lower bound of order 𝑞𝑋2𝜏 −𝑑 , which
degrades rapidly as smoothness grows or points cluster (Wendland 2005). For the Gaussian kernel, no polynomial
bound holds and 𝜆min (𝐾 ) decays exponentially. This is not an artifact of a bad basis; there is a theorem in the
way, made quantitative by Schaback (Schaback 1995).

Theorem 18.8 (uncertainty relation). Let 𝑘 be strictly positive definite, 𝑋 a set of distinct sites, and 𝑥 ∉ 𝑋 . Write
𝐾 ′ for the Gram matrix of 𝑋 ∪ {𝑥}. Then
                                                                     1
                                                 𝑃𝑋 (𝑥)2 =                        ≥ 𝜆min (𝐾 ′ ).
                                                               [(𝐾 ′ )−1 ]
                                                                             𝑥𝑥
  Accuracy and stability are therefore coupled: wherever the power function is small, the augmented Gram matrix
has a small eigenvalue.
   Assumptions. 𝑘 strictly positive definite; the sites of 𝑋 ∪ {𝑥} distinct. Proof status. complete; the trade-off principle is due to (Schaback
1995).

Proof. Order 𝐾 ′ with 𝑥 last, so 𝐾 ′ has blocks 𝐾 , 𝑘𝑋 (𝑥), and 𝑘(𝑥, 𝑥). The Schur complement of the block 𝐾 is
𝑘(𝑥, 𝑥)−𝑘𝑋 (𝑥)⊤ 𝐾 −1 𝑘𝑋 (𝑥) = 𝑃𝑋 (𝑥)2 , and the block-inverse formula identifies its reciprocal as the (𝑥, 𝑥) diagonal
entry of (𝐾 ′ )−1 . Since 𝐾 ′ is symmetric positive definite, every diagonal entry of (𝐾 ′ )−1 is at most 𝜆max ((𝐾 ′ )−1 ) =
1/𝜆min (𝐾 ′ ). Taking reciprocals gives 𝑃𝑋 (𝑥)2 ≥ 𝜆min (𝐾 ′ ).
                                                                                                                           
   Read the inequality as a conservation law. A kernel whose power function decays spectrally fast, such as the
Gaussian, forces 𝜆min of its Gram matrices to decay at least as fast, so spectral accuracy and well-conditioned
linear algebra cannot coexist in the standard basis. You may have either fast convergence in exact arithmetic or a
benign linear system in floating point, not both.
   The practical consequences center on the shape parameter 𝜖 , the inverse length-scale in 𝑘(𝑥, 𝑦) = 𝜑(𝜖‖𝑥 − 𝑦‖).
Small 𝜖 flattens the kernel, improves accuracy in exact arithmetic, and destroys conditioning; large 𝜖 localizes the
kernel, tames 𝐾 , and wastes the data. Flat kernels are dangerous precisely because the naive solve fails long before
the mathematical limit turns bad; in fact the 𝜖 → 0 limit of the interpolant is typically a polynomial interpolant,
and stable algorithms such as RBF-QR reach it by changing basis rather than by inverting 𝐾 (Fasshauer 2007).
When 𝑛 is also large, conditioning interacts with the iterative solvers and preconditioners of Chapter 12, Large-
Scale Kernel Machines; a Gram matrix that is nearly singular by design is the worst client an iterative method
can have.


18.6 Escaping the native space
The error theorem has a gap: it prices every target by its native-space norm, and for a target outside the native
space it goes silent. This matters most for smooth kernels, whose native spaces are smallest. What happens when
we interpolate a function rougher than the kernel expects? Sampling inequalities give the answer: convergence
survives, at the rate the target’s own smoothness supports.

Theorem 18.9 (rates outside the native space). Let Ω be a bounded Lipschitz domain and let 𝑘 have native space
norm-equivalent to 𝐻 𝜏 (Ω). Let 𝑓 ∈ 𝐻 𝛽 (Ω) with 𝑑/2 < 𝛽 ≤ 𝜏 , and let 𝑋 have fill distance ℎ and mesh ratio
𝜌 = ℎ/𝑞𝑋 . Then

                                             ‖𝑓 − 𝑠𝑓 ‖𝐿∞ (Ω) ≤ 𝐶 ℎ𝛽−𝑑/2 𝜌 𝜏 −𝛽 ‖𝑓 ‖𝐻 𝛽 (Ω) .
   Assumptions. Bounded Lipschitz domain, 𝛽 > 𝑑/2 so that point evaluations of 𝑓 are defined, ℎ below a threshold. Proof status. cited
from (Narcowich et al. 2005).

   The rate ℎ𝛽−𝑑/2 is the one a kernel of exactly the target’s smoothness would deliver, so the interpolant adapts
downward: using a kernel that is too smooth costs only the mesh-ratio factor 𝜌 𝜏 −𝛽 , which quasi-uniform designs
keep bounded, plus the conditioning penalty of the previous section. The condition 𝛽 > 𝑑/2 is not decoration;
below it, point values of 𝑓 are not even well defined and interpolation is the wrong question. Together with
the uncertainty relation, this theorem gives balanced advice: oversmooth kernels are statistically forgiving but
18.7 Schoenberg theory and conditional positive definiteness                                                            305



numerically brittle, and the Matern family with a moderate 𝜈 matched to the plausible roughness of the target is
usually the sound default.


18.7 Schoenberg theory and conditional positive definiteness
Radial kernels raise a structural question that we have so far dodged: which functions of distance are legitimate
kernels in the first place, on every ℝ𝑑 at once? The classical answer predates the RKHS literature and belongs to
Schoenberg.

Definition 18.10 (completely monotone function). A function 𝑔 ∈ 𝐶[0, ∞) ∩ 𝐶 ∞ (0, ∞) is completely monotone
when (−1)ℓ 𝑔 (ℓ) (𝑟) ≥ 0 for all 𝑟 > 0 and all integers ℓ ≥ 0: 𝑔 is nonnegative, nonincreasing, convex, and so on
through alternating signs of all derivatives.

Theorem 18.11 (Schoenberg). Let 𝑔 ∶ [0, ∞) → ℝ be continuous. The kernel 𝑘(𝑥, 𝑦) = 𝑔(‖𝑥 − 𝑦‖2 ) is positive
definite on ℝ𝑑 for every 𝑑 ≥ 1 if and only if 𝑔 is completely monotone; it is strictly positive definite on every ℝ𝑑 if and
only if 𝑔 is completely monotone and not constant.
   Assumptions. 𝑔 continuous on [0, ∞). Proof status. cited from (Schoenberg 1938).
                                                                                    2
   The theorem certifies the standard inventory at a glance: 𝑔(𝑟) = 𝑒 −𝜖 𝑟 gives the Gaussian, 𝑔(𝑟) = (1+𝑟)−1/2 the
inverse multiquadric, and any Laplace transform of a nonnegative measure qualifies. But it also excludes useful
functions: the multiquadric √1 + 𝑟 grows, and the thin-plate term 𝑟 log √𝑟 changes sign, yet both interpolate well
in practice. The fix is to relax positive definiteness on a finite-dimensional subspace.

Definition 18.12 (conditionally positive definite kernel). A symmetric kernel 𝑘 on ℝ𝑑 is conditionally positive
definite of order 𝑚 when for all distinct sites 𝑥1 , … , 𝑥𝑛 and all coefficients 𝑐 ≠ 0 satisfying ∑𝑖 𝑐𝑖 𝑝(𝑥𝑖 ) = 0 for
every polynomial 𝑝 of degree at most 𝑚 − 1, the quadratic form ∑𝑖,𝑗 𝑐𝑖 𝑐𝑗 𝑘(𝑥𝑖 , 𝑥𝑗 ) is strictly positive.
  Interpolation with a conditionally positive definite kernel augments the expansion with the polynomials it
exempts and imposes the moment conditions on the coefficients:
                                               𝑛
                                                                                 𝐾 𝑃 𝑐           𝑦
                                   𝑠(𝑥) = ∑ 𝑐𝑗 𝑘(𝑥, 𝑥𝑗 ) + ∑ 𝑏ℓ 𝑝ℓ (𝑥),         (𝑃 ⊤ 0 ) (𝑏 ) = ( 0 ) ,
                                             𝑗=1               ℓ
   where the columns of 𝑃 evaluate a basis of the exempt polynomials at the sites. Micchelli’s theorem supplies
the workhorse criterion: if 𝑔 ′ is completely monotone and non-constant, then 𝑔(‖𝑥 −𝑦‖2 ) is conditionally positive
definite of order one and the interpolation matrix is nonsingular for distinct sites, which covers the multiquadric
(Micchelli 1986). Thin-plate splines ‖𝑥 − 𝑦‖2 log‖𝑥 − 𝑦‖ and the polyharmonic family are conditionally positive
definite of higher order, and their augmented systems reproduce polynomials exactly: if the data come from a
polynomial of exempt degree, the interpolant returns it. This is the same semiparametric structure as the rep-
resenter theorem with unpenalized null space in Chapter 30, Smoothing Splines and Additive RKHS Models,
and the same device that universal kriging uses to model a mean drift in Chapter 31, Spatial and Spatiotempo-
ral Kernel Models. The moment conditions 𝑃 ⊤ 𝑐 = 0 are exactly what make the quadratic form, and hence the
native-space geometry, well defined modulo polynomials.


18.8 Worst case meets average case
We close the theory by making precise a claim implicit throughout: kernel interpolation is not merely a method
with good bounds, it is the best possible use of the data.

Proposition 18.13 (minimax optimal recovery). Fix a site set 𝑋 , a point 𝑥 , and the data map 𝑓                         ↦
(𝑓 (𝑥1 ), … , 𝑓 (𝑥𝑛 )). For any algorithm 𝐴, linear or not, that predicts 𝑓 (𝑥) from the data,

                                                sup |𝑓 (𝑥) − 𝐴(𝑓 (𝑥1 ), … , 𝑓 (𝑥𝑛 ))| ≥ 𝑃𝑋 (𝑥),
                                             ‖𝑓 ‖ℋ ≤1
                                                   𝑘
306                                                                                            18 Kernel Interpolation and Approximation Theory



   and the kernel interpolant attains this bound. Interpolation is therefore minimax optimal among all algorithms
using the same data.
      Assumptions. 𝑘 strictly positive definite, distinct sites. Proof status. sketched.

    The argument is a two-point trick. Let 𝑟𝑥 be the error representer and set 𝑓± = ±𝑟𝑥 /‖𝑟𝑥 ‖. Both functions
vanish at every site, so any algorithm receives identical, all-zero data and returns the same prediction for both;
yet 𝑓+ (𝑥) − 𝑓− (𝑥) = 2𝑃𝑋 (𝑥), so on at least one of them the algorithm errs by 𝑃𝑋 (𝑥) or more. The interpolant of
zero data is zero, whose error on 𝑓± is exactly 𝑃𝑋 (𝑥).
    Now place this beside the probabilistic reading. Under a Gaussian process prior with covariance 𝑘 , the pos-
terior mean given noise-free data is the kernel interpolant, and the posterior standard deviation at 𝑥 is 𝑃𝑋 (𝑥)
(Rasmussen and Williams 2006). The identical formulas thus answer two different questions: the worst case over
a native-space ball, and the average case under a Gaussian prior, a correspondence running through the spline
literature since (Wahba 1990). Nothing is mystical here; both derivations optimize the same quadratic functional.
But the interpretations diverge exactly where practice needs care: the worst-case bound requires 𝑓 in the native
space with known norm, while the Bayesian error bar requires the prior to be honest, and GP sample paths them-
selves lie outside the native space almost surely. The acquisition rules of Chapter 50, Kernelized Bandits and
Bayesian Optimization consume the same mean and error bar, and inherit whichever reading one can defend.
    One refinement is worth flagging: superconvergence. For targets smoother than the generic native-space ele-
ment, in the sense of lying in the range of the kernel’s integral operator, the 𝐿2 error rate roughly doubles, from
ℎ𝜏 toward ℎ2𝜏 -type behavior, because the error functional then acts through the operator a second time (Wend-
land 2005). The generic bound of the power function is sharp over the whole ball, but the ball’s smoother core
converges faster; the source conditions of Chapter 16, Mercer’s Theorem, Spectra, and Rates tell the same story
in spectral language.

18.10 Common mistakes and practical implications
    • Interpolation is optimal for noiseless data only. With observation noise the minimum-norm interpolant
      chases the noise, and the correct estimator is the regularized one; the power function then understates the
      error because it prices bias but not variance.
    • The error bound 𝑃𝑋 (𝑥)‖𝑓 ‖ is vacuous when 𝑓 is outside the native space, and native spaces of smooth
      kernels are far smaller than intuition suggests; a Gaussian kernel’s native space contains no function with
      a kink (Steinwart and Christmann 2008). Check target smoothness before quoting spectral rates.
    • Do not report accuracy without conditioning. By the uncertainty relation, a power function near machine
      precision forces 𝜆min (𝐾 ) near machine precision, and the printed solution of 𝐾 𝑐 = 𝑦 may carry no correct
      digits. Report ℎ𝑋 ,Ω , 𝑞𝑋 , and an estimate of 𝜆min or the condition number together.
    • Shrinking the shape parameter until the error on a test grid stops improving is a trap: the apparent opti-
      mum often sits where rounding error and truncated convergence cancel. Stable evaluations of the flat limit
      change basis instead of inverting 𝐾 (Fasshauer 2007).
    • Rates are driven by the fill distance, not the sample size. Clustered designs waste points; near-uniform or
      greedy power-function designs achieve the same ℎ with far fewer sites, at bounded mesh ratio.
    • Conditionally positive definite kernels require their polynomial block. Dropping the moment conditions
      𝑃 ⊤ 𝑐 = 0 for thin-plate or multiquadric interpolation produces a system that may be singular and an inter-
      polant without polynomial reproduction.
    • The GP posterior standard deviation and the power function are the same formula, but their guarantees dif-
      fer. Quoting a worst-case bound requires a norm estimate for the target; quoting a credible interval requires
      defending the prior. Choose one and say which.


18.11 Summary and further reading
Noiseless kernel interpolation solves 𝐾 𝑐 = 𝑦 and returns the unique minimum-norm interpolant in the native
space, the limit of kernel ridge regression as regularization vanishes and the common core of kriging and spline in-
terpolation. The native space of a translation-invariant kernel is a Fourier-weighted smoothness class: Sobolev for
Matern kernels, a small analytic class for the Gaussian. The power function 𝑃𝑋 (𝑥)2 = 𝑘(𝑥, 𝑥)−𝑘𝑋 (𝑥)⊤ 𝐾 −1 𝑘𝑋 (𝑥)
is the norm of the pointwise error functional, yields the sharp bound |𝑓 (𝑥) − 𝑠𝑓 (𝑥)| ≤ 𝑃𝑋 (𝑥)‖𝑓 ‖, and coincides
with the noise-free GP posterior standard deviation, so worst-case and average-case analyses share their formulas
while differing in guarantees. Fill distance drives convergence, with rate ℎ𝜏 −𝑑/2 in the sup norm for smoothness 𝜏
and spectral rates for the Gaussian; separation radius drives stability, and the Schur-complement uncertainty rela-
tion 𝑃𝑋 (𝑥)2 ≥ 𝜆min (𝐾 ′ ) shows accuracy and conditioning cannot be had together. Sampling inequalities extend
the theory to targets rougher than the native space at their own natural rate, and Schoenberg’s completely mono-
tone characterization, with its conditionally positive definite extension, settles which radial functions interpolate
legitimately.
    For further reading, Wendland’s monograph (Wendland 2005) is the standard rigorous account of native
spaces, error estimates, and stability; Fasshauer (Fasshauer 2007) gives a computational treatment with ex-
tensive shape-parameter practice. Schaback’s trade-off principle appears in his 1995 paper (Schaback 1995),
and the escape from the native space is due to Narcowich, Ward, and Wendland (Narcowich et al. 2005). The
classical roots are Schoenberg’s 1938 characterization (Schoenberg 1938), Micchelli’s 1986 interpolation theorem
(Micchelli 1986), and Aronszajn’s 1950 theory of reproducing kernels (Aronszajn 1950). Wahba (Wahba 1990)
connects splines, kriging, and Bayesian readings; Rasmussen and Williams (Rasmussen and Williams 2006) give
the GP side, and Steinwart and Christmann (Steinwart and Christmann 2008) the fine structure of Gaussian
RKHSs; Caponnetto and De Vito (Caponnetto and De Vito 2007) develop the noisy statistical counterpart of
these rates.

CHAPTER 19




Universality, Capacity, and
Consistency

      Ten million labeled examples cannot rescue a learner whose hypothesis class is blind to the
   truth: if every function it can represent misclassifies a region of positive probability, more data
   only makes it confident about the wrong answer. So before any argument about noise or sample
   size there is a prior question, and it is a question about the kernel: which targets can the RKHS
   approach at all? This chapter answers it three ways. Universality makes the qualitative answer
   precise, an RKHS dense in the continuous functions, and we prove it for the Gaussian kernel and
   refute it for polynomials. Consistency cashes the license: SVMs with a universal kernel and a prop-
   erly scheduled penalty converge to the Bayes risk for every distribution. Capacity then presents
   the bill, because a space dense enough to approximate everything must be measured by covering
   numbers and eigenvalue decay before it yields a rate, and no rate is uniform over everything the
   space can reach.




19.1 The approximation question learning cannot skip
Every generalization bound we have proved so far controls the gap between empirical and population risk over
a fixed class. None of them says a word about whether the class contains anything worth converging to. To see
why that omission is fatal, split the excess risk of an estimator 𝑓𝑛̂ chosen from a hypothesis class ℱ :

                             𝑅(𝑓𝑛̂ ) − 𝑅∗ = 𝑅(𝑓𝑛̂ ) − inf 𝑅(𝑓 ) + inf 𝑅(𝑓 ) − 𝑅∗ ,
                                            ⏟⏟⏟⏟⏟⏟⏟⏟⏟⏟⏟⏟⏟⏟⏟⏟⏟
                                                     𝑓 ∈ℱ        ⏟⏟⏟⏟⏟⏟⏟⏟⏟⏟⏟⏟⏟⏟⏟
                                                                  𝑓 ∈ℱ
                                                estimation error    approximation error

  where 𝑅∗ is the Bayes risk. The estimation error is the statistical term: it is random, it shrinks with 𝑛, and the
tools of Chapter 14, Learning Theory in RKHS Balls and Chapter 15, VC Theory and Generalization bound it. The
approximation error is deterministic. It does not depend on the data, it does not shrink with 𝑛, and no algorithm
operating inside ℱ can reduce it. A method can be universally consistent only if this deterministic floor can be
driven to zero, which for kernel methods means the RKHS, or the union of its balls as regularization is relaxed,
must come arbitrarily close to the relevant targets (Steinwart and Christmann 2008).
312                                                                                                  19 Universality, Capacity, and Consistency



   Closeness in which norm? For bounded losses that are Lipschitz in their function argument, uniform approx-
imation on the input space suffices: if ‖𝑓 − 𝑔‖∞ ≤ 𝜀 then the risks of 𝑓 and 𝑔 differ by at most a constant times 𝜀 .
This is why density of the RKHS in the space of continuous functions, with respect to the uniform norm, is the
right qualitative demand. A dense RKHS is a license: it guarantees the approximation error vanishes for every
continuous target, hence for every distribution once we account for the density of continuous functions in the
relevant 𝐿𝑝 spaces.
   Classification needs one more link in the chain, since the 0-1 loss is neither convex nor Lipschitz. The link is
calibration: the excess 0-1 risk of the sign of 𝑓 is controlled by the excess hinge or logistic risk of 𝑓 , so a density
argument carried out for the surrogate transfers to the classifier (Steinwart and Christmann 2008). With that
reduction in hand, the rest of the chapter makes the license precise, shows which kernels hold it, and then asks
what it costs.


19.2 Universal kernels
Which kernels generate an RKHS that is dense in the continuous functions? The definition fixes the arena: a
compact input space, the uniform norm.

Definition 19.1 (universal kernel on a compact space). Let 𝒳 be a compact metric space and 𝑘 a continuous
positive definite kernel on 𝒳 with RKHS ℋ𝑘 . The kernel 𝑘 is universal if ℋ𝑘 is dense in 𝐶(𝒳 ) with respect to
the uniform norm: for every 𝑓 ∈ 𝐶(𝒳 ) and every 𝜀 > 0 there exists 𝑔 ∈ ℋ𝑘 with ‖𝑓 − 𝑔‖∞ ≤ 𝜀 . When the input
space is not compact, we call 𝑘 cc-universal if this density holds on every compact subset, which is density in the
topology of compact convergence.

19.2.1 Steinwart's criterion and Taylor-series kernels
How would one ever verify density in 𝐶(𝒳 )? The classical engine is the Stone-Weierstrass theorem: a subalgebra
of 𝐶(𝒳 ) that contains the constants and separates points is dense. The strategy, due to Steinwart, is to exhibit
inside the RKHS a set of functions whose span is such an algebra (Steinwart 2001). The argument is honest but
has a step worth flagging: Stone-Weierstrass certifies density of the span of the feature coordinates, and one must
then check that every finite linear combination of those coordinates genuinely belongs to the RKHS, which holds
because finite combinations of feature coordinates are RKHS elements with finite norm. Density of a subset of
ℋ𝑘 in 𝐶(𝒳 ) then transfers to ℋ𝑘 itself.
                                                                                                          ∞
Theorem 19.2 (Taylor-series kernels are universal). Let 0 < 𝑟 ≤ ∞ and let 𝑓 (𝑡) = ∑𝑖=0 𝑎𝑖 𝑡 𝑖 converge on (−𝑟, 𝑟)
with 𝑎𝑖 > 0 for all 𝑖 ≥ 0. Then for every compact 𝒳 contained in the open Euclidean ball of radius √𝑟 in ℝ𝑑 , the
kernel 𝑘(𝑥, 𝑦) = 𝑓 (⟨𝑥, 𝑦⟩) is universal on 𝒳 . In particular the exponential kernel 𝑘(𝑥, 𝑦) = exp(⟨𝑥, 𝑦⟩) is universal
on every compact subset of ℝ𝑑 .
   Assumptions. All Taylor coefficients strictly positive; 𝒳 compact inside the convergence region. Proof status. Sketched below; complete
proof cited from (Steinwart 2001).

Proof. The features of 𝑘 are the monomials 𝑥 ↦ √𝑎𝑖 𝑥 𝛼 rescaled by multinomial weights, so the span of the
feature coordinates is the algebra of all polynomials on 𝒳 , which contains constants (the 𝑖 = 0 term, since 𝑎0 > 0)
and separates points (the degree-one terms, since 𝑎1 > 0). Stone-Weierstrass gives density of the polynomials
in 𝐶(𝒳 ); finite combinations of features lie in ℋ𝑘 , so ℋ𝑘 is dense. The step we do not carry out here is the
verification that the series expansion defines a valid feature map into ℓ2 on the stated domain.
                                                                                                                  

Remark 19.3 (what Stone-Weierstrass does and does not deliver). Two honest caveats keep the argument from
proving more than it can. First, Stone-Weierstrass concerns the uniform norm only. It grants, for each target 𝑓 and
each 𝜀 , some 𝑔𝜀 ∈ ℋ𝑘 within 𝜀 in ‖⋅‖∞ ; it says nothing about ‖𝑔𝜀 ‖ℋ𝑘 , and for targets outside the RKHS this norm
must diverge as 𝜀 → 0, since a uniformly bounded ball of ℋ𝑘 is compact in 𝐶(𝒳 ) and hence closed. Universality
is compatible with, indeed forces, arbitrarily expensive approximants. Second, the theorem needs an algebra:
closure of the feature span under products is a genuine hypothesis, satisfied by monomials and by trigonometric
19.2 Universal kernels                                                                                                            313



families, and not by an arbitrary feature list. Both caveats foreshadow the second half of this chapter: the price
of an approximant is a capacity statement, not a density statement.

19.2.2 The Micchelli-Xu-Zhang characterization
Sufficient conditions leave a gap: is there a criterion that decides universality exactly? Micchelli, Xu, and Zhang
closed the question for kernels given by a continuous feature expansion (Micchelli et al. 2006).

Theorem 19.4 (characterization of universality, Micchelli-Xu-Zhang). Let 𝒳 be a compact metric space and
𝑘(𝑥, 𝑦) = ∑𝑖∈𝐼 𝜑𝑖 (𝑥)𝜑𝑖 (𝑦) a continuous kernel with continuous features 𝜑𝑖 . Then 𝑘 is universal on 𝒳 if and only if
span{𝜑𝑖 ∶ 𝑖 ∈ 𝐼 } is dense in 𝐶(𝒳 ). Equivalently, 𝑘 is universal if and only if the only finite signed Borel measure 𝜈 on
𝒳 with ∫ 𝑘(⋅, 𝑦) 𝑑𝜈(𝑦) = 0 is 𝜈 = 0: universality is injectivity of the kernel embedding on finite signed measures.
          𝒳
   Assumptions. Compact metric input space; continuous kernel and features; the expansion converges uniformly on 𝒳 ×𝒳 . Proof status.
Cited from (Micchelli et al. 2006).

   The second formulation is the one to remember, because it converts a density statement into an injectivity
statement, and injectivity statements about measures are exactly what the characteristic-kernel theory of Chapter
41, Mean Embeddings, MMD, and Characteristic Kernels trades in. We exploit the parallel in the next section.

19.2.3 Two worked verdicts
The criterion delivers concrete verdicts. First the positive one.

Proposition 19.5 (the Gaussian kernel is universal). For every 𝛾 > 0 and every compact 𝒳 ⊂ ℝ𝑑 , the Gaussian
kernel 𝑘(𝑥, 𝑦) = exp(−𝛾 ‖𝑥 − 𝑦‖2 ) is universal on 𝒳 .
   Assumptions. Compact Euclidean input set; any fixed bandwidth. Proof status. Sketched below; complete proofs cited from (Steinwart
2001) and (Micchelli et al. 2006).

Proof. Factor exp(−𝛾 ‖𝑥 − 𝑦‖2 ) = exp(−𝛾 ‖𝑥‖2 ) exp(−𝛾 ‖𝑦‖2 ) exp(2𝛾 ⟨𝑥, 𝑦⟩). The middle factor exp(2𝛾 ⟨𝑥, 𝑦⟩) is
a Taylor-series kernel with all coefficients (2𝛾 )𝑖 /𝑖! positive, hence universal by the theorem above. Multiplying
every function of its RKHS by the fixed function 𝑥 ↦ exp(−𝛾 ‖𝑥‖2 ), which is continuous, strictly positive, and
bounded away from zero on the compact set 𝒳 , is a homeomorphism of 𝐶(𝒳 ) onto itself, so it preserves density
of the image. The image is exactly the RKHS of the Gaussian kernel restricted to 𝒳 .
                                                                                                                 
   Now the negative one, with a complete proof, because it shows what failure of universality looks like struc-
turally rather than pointwise.

Proposition 19.6 (polynomial kernels of fixed degree are not universal). Let 𝑚 ∈ ℕ and 𝑐 ≥ 0, and let 𝑘(𝑥, 𝑦) =
(⟨𝑥, 𝑦⟩ + 𝑐)𝑚 on any compact 𝒳 ⊂ ℝ𝑑 containing infinitely many points. Then 𝑘 is not universal on 𝒳 .
   Assumptions. Fixed finite degree; infinite compact input set. Proof status. Complete.

Proof. Expanding the binomial shows every function 𝑔 ∈ ℋ𝑘 is a polynomial of total degree at most 𝑚 restricted
to 𝒳 , so ℋ𝑘 is contained in a linear space 𝒫𝑚 of dimension at most (𝑑+𝑚𝑚 ), a finite number. A finite-dimensional
subspace of a normed space is closed, so the uniform closure of ℋ𝑘 is contained in 𝒫𝑚 itself. It remains to note
that 𝐶(𝒳 ) ≠ 𝒫𝑚 . Since 𝒳 is infinite, we may pick distinct points 𝑥0 , … , 𝑥𝑁 ∈ 𝒳 with 𝑁 = (𝑑+𝑚 𝑚 ); by Urysohn’s
lemma there are continuous functions taking arbitrary prescribed values at these 𝑁 +1 points, so 𝐶(𝒳 ) restricted
to them has dimension 𝑁 + 1, while 𝒫𝑚 restricted to any point set has dimension at most 𝑁 . Hence some con-
tinuous function stays at uniform distance bounded away from zero from all of 𝒫𝑚 , and ℋ𝑘 is not dense.
                                                                                                                
   The failure is not about any single hard target; it is dimensional. A fixed-degree polynomial RKHS is a closed
finite-dimensional slice of 𝐶(𝒳 ), and no amount of data moves an estimator off that slice. This is the function-
space face of the moment blindness seen in Chapter 41, Mean Embeddings, MMD, and Characteristic Kernels,
where the degree-two polynomial kernel could not distinguish distributions agreeing on their first two mo-
ments.
314                                                                                                 19 Universality, Capacity, and Consistency



19.3 The universality hierarchy
On non-compact spaces such as ℝ𝑑 , “dense in the continuous functions” splits into inequivalent readings de-
pending on which continuous functions and which norm. Three have become standard (Sriperumbudur et al.
2011).

Definition 19.7 (c0-, cc-, and Lp-universality). Let 𝒳 be a locally compact Hausdorff space and 𝑘 a bounded
continuous kernel. The kernel is c0-universal if 𝑘(⋅, 𝑥) vanishes at infinity for each 𝑥 and ℋ𝑘 is dense in 𝐶0 (𝒳 ),
the continuous functions vanishing at infinity, under the uniform norm. It is cc-universal if ℋ𝑘 is dense in 𝐶(𝑍 )
for every compact 𝑍 ⊂ 𝒳 . For 1 ≤ 𝑝 < ∞, it is Lp-universal if ℋ𝑘 is dense in 𝐿𝑝 (𝜇) for every Borel probability
measure 𝜇 on 𝒳 .
      The notions are ordered, and the order is worth displaying:


  c0 -universal ⟹ cc-universal,               𝐿1 -universal ⟹ characteristic,                c0 -universal ⟹ characteristic,

   with none of the arrows reversible in general, while on a compact space cc-universality collapses to the plain
universality of the previous section and already implies the characteristic property. For the important subfamily
                                                         ∞         2
of radial kernels on ℝ𝑑 , those of the form 𝑘(𝑥, 𝑦) = ∫ 𝑒 −𝑡‖𝑥−𝑦‖ 𝑑𝜂(𝑡) for a finite measure 𝜂, the hierarchy flat-
                                                         0
tens completely: cc-universality, c0-universality, the characteristic property, and strict positive definiteness are all
equivalent, and all hold as soon as 𝜂 is not concentrated at zero (Sriperumbudur et al. 2011). This is the formal
sense in which “any reasonable radial kernel works” for the tests of Chapter 42, Kernel Hypothesis Testing, and it
explains why practitioners rarely see the hierarchy’s fine structure: the kernels that expose it, like the sinc kernel
below, are exactly the ones with constrained spectral support. The map that organizes the whole picture is the
mean embedding 𝑃 ↦ 𝜇𝑃 = ∫ 𝑘(⋅, 𝑥) 𝑑𝑃(𝑥) of Chapter 41, Mean Embeddings, MMD, and Characteristic Kernels:
a kernel is characteristic exactly when this embedding is injective on probability measures. Universality demands
injectivity on the larger space of finite signed measures, by the Micchelli-Xu-Zhang criterion, so the hierarchy of
function-space densities is mirrored by a hierarchy of measure-space injectivities (Sriperumbudur et al. 2011).

Proposition 19.8 (universal implies characteristic). Let 𝒳 be compact and 𝑘 universal on 𝒳 . Then 𝑘 is charac-
teristic: 𝜇𝑃 = 𝜇𝑄 implies 𝑃 = 𝑄 for Borel probability measures 𝑃, 𝑄 .
   Assumptions. Compact input space; bounded continuous universal kernel. Proof status. Sketched below; full statement and non-
compact extensions cited from (Sriperumbudur and Lanckriet 2010) and (Sriperumbudur et al. 2011).

Proof. If 𝜇𝑃 = 𝜇𝑄 then 𝔼𝑃 [𝑔] = 𝔼𝑄 [𝑔] for every 𝑔 ∈ ℋ𝑘 , by the reproducing property and linearity. Given
𝑓 ∈ 𝐶(𝒳 ) and 𝜀 > 0, universality supplies 𝑔 ∈ ℋ𝑘 with ‖𝑓 − 𝑔‖∞ ≤ 𝜀 , so the expectations of 𝑓 under 𝑃 and
𝑄 differ by at most 2𝜀 . Letting 𝜀 → 0 shows all continuous functions integrate identically, which on a compact
metric space forces 𝑃 = 𝑄 by the Riesz representation theorem.
                                                                                                             
  The converse fails in general: characteristic kernels need only tell probability measures apart, and the differ-
ence of two probability measures is a signed measure of total mass zero, a strictly smaller test class than all signed
measures. On ℝ𝑑 , however, the two notions come close to merging for the kernels we use most, and the meeting
point is Bochner’s theorem from Chapter 28, Translation-Invariant, Semigroup, and Probabilistic Kernels.

Theorem 19.9 (spectral support criterion, translation-invariant case). Let 𝑘(𝑥, 𝑦) = 𝜓 (𝑥 − 𝑦) be a bounded
continuous translation-invariant kernel on ℝ𝑑 with Bochner representation 𝜓 (𝑧) = ∫ 𝑑 𝑒 −𝑖⟨𝑧,𝜔⟩ 𝑑Λ(𝜔) for a finite
                                                                                                      ℝ
non-negative measure Λ. Then 𝑘 is characteristic if and only if the support of Λ is all of ℝ𝑑 . Moreover, for such
kernels full spectral support is also equivalent to c0-universality when 𝜓 ∈ 𝐶0 (ℝ𝑑 ), so the characteristic and universal
properties coincide in this class.
   Assumptions. Translation invariance; boundedness and continuity; finiteness of the spectral measure. Proof status. Cited from (Sripe-
rumbudur and Lanckriet 2010) and (Sriperumbudur et al. 2011).

  The Fourier reading is direct: the embedding of a distribution through 𝑘 stores its characteristic function
reweighted by Λ, so the kernel sees exactly those frequencies that Λ charges. The Gaussian kernel has a Gaussian
19.4 Universal consistency of kernel machines                                                                                       315



spectral density, positive everywhere, hence is characteristic and c0-universal; the same holds for Matern and
Laplace kernels. The sinc kernel has spectral measure supported on a bounded interval, misses all high frequen-
cies, and is neither. Every verdict of this section is thus a statement about where a kernel’s spectral mass lives, a
theme continued when we count eigenvalues below.


19.4 Universal consistency of kernel machines
Density is a statement about function spaces. Consistency is a statement about algorithms. The bridge deserves
a careful definition before the theorem that crosses it.

Definition 19.10 (universal consistency). A learning method producing 𝑓𝑛̂ from 𝑛 i.i.d. samples is universally
consistent for a loss 𝐿 if for every Borel probability distribution 𝑃 on 𝒳 × 𝒴 , the risk converges to the Bayes risk
in probability: 𝑅(𝑓𝑛̂ ) → 𝑅∗ as 𝑛 → ∞. The convergence must hold for every 𝑃 ; no smoothness, margin, or source
condition may be assumed.

Theorem 19.11 (universal consistency of SVMs, cited). Let 𝒳 ⊂ ℝ𝑑 be compact and 𝑘 a universal kernel on
𝒳 . Consider the SVM of Chapter 5, Support Vector Machines with hinge loss and regularization parameters 𝜆𝑛 . If
𝜆𝑛 → 0 and 𝑛𝜆𝑛2 → ∞, then the SVM classifier is universally consistent. Analogous statements hold for regularized
least squares with its own admissible schedules.
    Assumptions. Compact input space; bounded universal kernel; the stated schedule for 𝜆𝑛 ; i.i.d. sampling. Proof status. Cited from
(Steinwart 2001) and (Steinwart and Christmann 2008); least-squares rates under additional assumptions cited from (Steinwart and Scovel
2009).

   The proof strategy is the decomposition of the opening section, run along a schedule. Write 𝑓𝜆 for the popula-

in Chapter 14, Learning Theory in RKHS Balls control the estimation bracket, with a deviation that grows as 𝜆
